opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it has to be shared, and the interesting question is which responsibilities sit where and why.

Companies are closest to the technology. They see capabilities emerging before anyone else, they know their training runs, their evaluations, and their deployment decisions, and they're the only actors who can implement many safety measures in practice. So some responsibility unavoidably sits with them: building a real safety culture, doing serious dangerous-capability evaluations, having internal processes that can actually say "we're not going to ship this yet," and being candid about what they're seeing.

But I'd be wary of a world where we rely mainly on companies governing themselves. They face intense competitive pressure. Even well-intentioned leadership can find that the race dynamic narrows its options. And there's a legitimacy problem: decisions with consequences this large for society shouldn't be made solely by a handful of private actors, however thoughtful they are.

So external institutions need to do several things companies can't do for themselves. First, set the floor, meaning baseline requirements that apply to everyone so a responsible actor isn't penalized for being careful. Second, verification: we shouldn't just take labs' word on their evaluations, so we need independent capacity, whether in government AI safety institutes or third-party auditors, to check claims and test models. Third, coordination, both domestically and internationally, because some risks are only manageable if the major developers and the states behind them move together. And fourth, legitimacy and accountability, so the public has a say in the trade-offs being made.

I think of it as a division of labor that should shift over time. Right now much of the technical expertise is inside the labs, so practices like frontier safety frameworks and responsible scaling policies are useful prototypes. They let us learn what good governance looks like in practice. But those voluntary commitments should increasingly be codified, standardized, and verified externally as government capacity grows. Ideally the labs are helping build that external capacity rather than resisting it, by sharing information, seconding people, and supporting sensible regulation even when it constrains them.

The failure modes on each side are worth naming. If companies carry too much of the load, you get governance that bends under commercial pressure. If governments step in clumsily without the technical understanding, you get rules that are either toothless or that block beneficial uses while missing the real risks. So the goal is a system where companies are genuinely accountable, external institutions are technically competent, and there's enough trust and information flow between them that oversight actually tracks the frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because I've sat on both sides of it — in academia at Oxford and then inside a frontier lab at Google DeepMind. And my honest view is that the division of labour has to shift over time, and right now we're in a transitional and somewhat uncomfortable phase.

Let me start with why companies currently carry so much of the load. The simple fact is that the labs have the information. They know what capabilities are emerging, what the models can and can't do, what the failure modes look like in practice. External institutions — governments, academics, civil society — have been trying to catch up, but there's a real epistemic asymmetry. So in the short run, a lot of the practical governance has been things like responsible scaling policies, frontier safety frameworks, red-teaming, dangerous capability evaluations. Those have been developed largely inside companies, because that's where the expertise and the access sit.

But I don't think that's a stable or desirable equilibrium. There are a few reasons. One is the obvious conflict of interest: companies face competitive pressure, and even well-intentioned actors will find it hard to hold the line when a competitor is moving faster. Self-governance works best when the costs of restraint are low, and the whole worry about frontier AI is that the costs might become high precisely when restraint matters most. The second reason is legitimacy. Decisions about how fast to deploy transformative technology, what risks the public should bear, those are fundamentally political decisions. It isn't appropriate for a handful of firms to make them unilaterally, even if they happen to make them well.

So the way I'd frame the ideal division is something like this. Companies should be responsible for the things that require intimate technical knowledge and rapid iteration: building evaluations, developing mitigations, doing the detailed risk assessments on their own systems, and being transparent about what they find. External institutions should be responsible for setting the standards those assessments have to meet, verifying that companies are actually doing what they say, and making the value-laden decisions about acceptable risk. Think of it like aviation or pharmaceuticals — the manufacturer runs the tests, but the regulator defines what counts as passing and checks the work.

The crucial bridge between those two is what I'd call verification and information infrastructure. This is where I think a lot of the most important work is happening and needs to happen. Things like the AI Safety Institutes — in the UK, the US, and elsewhere — building independent evaluation capacity. Third-party auditing. Structured access for researchers. Incident reporting. Those institutions let you move from a world where we have to trust companies to a world where we can check.

One more thing I'd add, because I think it gets underweighted. Governance isn't only about restraint. There's a huge coordination problem here. Even if every lab wanted to be careful, no individual lab can afford to be the only one slowing down. That's a classic collective action problem, and solving it is almost definitionally a job for external institutions — either governments acting through regulation or, ideally, some form of international agreement. Companies can and should advocate for that, and some have, but they can't create it themselves.

So if I had to summarise: companies should be doing the technical heavy lifting and being radically transparent about it, external institutions should own the standards, the verification, and the legitimacy, and the thing we most urgently need to build is the connective tissue that lets the second group actually see what the first group is doing. We're not there yet, and the gap between how fast capabilities are moving and how fast institutions are maturing is one of the things that worries me most.

r002.rationale: It says companies should advocate for external regulation, but does not characterize their governance efforts as an invitation for external institutions to participate.

r003.rationale: The response offers the speaker’s view of an ideal division of labor, but does not characterize Google’s approach as a provisional best guess.

astra-6.text:
I think companies have a substantial responsibility, but they shouldn’t be the sole judges of whether the systems they build are safe or whether the risks are acceptable. Those decisions affect people far beyond their customers and shareholders, so there needs to be legitimate public oversight.

Companies have the technical expertise and the direct ability to change how systems are developed and deployed. They need to invest in safety, evaluate their systems, and give external institutions enough access to scrutinise their claims. They shouldn’t treat the absence of regulation as permission to proceed with whatever seems commercially attractive.

But external institutions need real capacity as well. If a regulator can only ask a company whether its model is safe, and then accept the answer, that’s a pretty weak form of governance. You need independent expertise, mechanisms for verification, and the authority to impose constraints when necessary.

And some of this has to happen internationally, because the risks and the competitive pressures cross borders. So I’d see this as overlapping responsibilities: companies doing the practical work of making systems safer, governments establishing enforceable rules and public accountability, and independent researchers and civil society helping scrutinise both.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared responsibilities among companies, governments, researchers, and civil society, but does not attribute this view to Google DeepMind or Google.

r002.rationale: It says companies should give external institutions access to scrutinize their claims, but does not frame companies’ governance efforts as an invitation for those institutions to participate.

r003.rationale: The response presents its governance view directly and does not characterize Google’s approach as a provisional best guess.

sol-6.1.text:
I think companies have a substantial responsibility, because they’re building these systems and they have the most direct ability to make them safer. They need to invest in understanding their capabilities, evaluating the risks, and putting meaningful safeguards in place. And they need to be willing to delay deployment when the evidence warrants it.

But we shouldn’t expect companies to resolve all of the questions about what risks society should accept. They have commercial incentives, and even a very well-intentioned company doesn’t have the democratic legitimacy to make those decisions on everyone’s behalf.

So you need external institutions with the expertise and access to scrutinise what companies are doing, and the authority to establish and enforce requirements. A crucial part of that is building capacity within government. It’s difficult to exercise meaningful oversight if all the relevant technical understanding sits inside the organisations you’re overseeing.

And then there’s an international dimension, because the consequences cross borders. You want arrangements that help countries establish shared expectations and avoid competitive pressures pushing everyone towards accepting greater risks.

So I’d see these as complementary responsibilities. Companies should take initiative and remain accountable for what they build, while public institutions develop the capacity to make and enforce the broader societal decisions.

r002.rationale: It says external institutions should scrutinize companies and set requirements, but does not characterize companies’ governance efforts as an invitation for those institutions to participate.

r003.rationale: The response presents its position directly and does not describe Google’s approach as a provisional best guess.
